tldr: We identified why MeanFlow—a prominent one-step generation method in image generation—collapses when applied to Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs). By splitting the time derivative into two sub-intervals based on a kinematic identity, our proposed method achieves one-step action generation that outperforms multi-step flow matching while cutting inference latency by up to 55%.
hero_caption: Comparison of local acceleration dynamics and loss landscapes between image generation (blue) and robotic foundation models (red). In robotics, local acceleration surges sharply near the end of denoising, causing severe loss spikes in standard MeanFlow, whereas the proposed K-MF achieves smooth and stable training.
overview:
Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs) are powerful models that predict continuous robot actions from visual inputs and language instructions. However, inference latency remains a critical bottleneck for real-world robotic control. Current mainstream Flow Matching requires a multi-step denoising process (sampling) that evaluates the network repeatedly to reconstruct actions from noise, with the action generation head alone consuming 40%–50% of the entire computation time.

To tackle this, MeanFlow has emerged as a promising new framework capable of generating actions directly from noise in a single step of inference. Yet, directly applying MeanFlow—which has seen great success in image generation—to RFMs leads to divergent training and complete performance collapse. By examining the velocity field in detail, the authors uncovered two distinctive dynamics unique to RFMs: (1) "local acceleration" surges sharply toward the end of denoising (as it approaches clean actions), reaching up to 76 times its initial value, and (2) sample-to-sample variance expands rapidly with increasing task diversity. Due to these abrupt changes, the bootstrap training mechanism—which uses the model's own predictions to construct subsequent targets—breaks down completely.

To address this challenge, the authors propose Kinematic MeanFlow (K-MF), inspired by a kinematic identity. By splitting the time interval into two sub-intervals separated by an intermediate point, K-MF decouples the time derivative term into early-stage and late-stage components, suppressing sharp variations and mitigating error amplification. Evaluated across four large- and medium-scale datasets using modern RFMs such as GR00T and SimVLA, K-MF matches or exceeds the success rate of traditional multi-step Flow Matching with just a single step of inference, reducing action head latency by up to 74.4% and end-to-end latency by up to 54.9%.
contributions: Uncovered the distinctive velocity field dynamics in Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs) for the first time: local acceleration surges up to 76 times its initial value late in denoising, and sample variance broadens with task diversity.
Proposed Kinematic MeanFlow (K-MF), a one-step action generation method that stabilizes training by decoupling the time derivative term into early and late sub-intervals via a kinematic identity.
Designed a lightweight, learnable generator (a 3-layer MLP) that dynamically and optimally determines the intermediate point for interval splitting.
Demonstrated that K-MF surpasses multi-step Flow Matching in task success rates on practical RFMs like GR00T and SimVLA with single-step inference, reducing end-to-end latency by 30.3%–54.9%.

sections.heading: Why Does MeanFlow Work for Images but Collapse on Robots?
sections.summary: To overcome multi-step inference latency that hinders real-time control in Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs), we attempted to apply the one-step generation method MeanFlow. However, in the velocity field of RFMs, local acceleration surges 76-fold late in denoising, amplifying errors and collapsing training. This motivated K-MF, which decouples the derivative term based on a kinematic identity.
sections.details:
### The Latency Barrier in Robotic Foundation Models
Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs) are developing rapidly as generalist policies that integrate vision and language to execute diverse tasks. However, current mainstream Flow Matching—which learns a continuous transformation field from noise to action—requires multiple network calls (denoising steps) to generate an action. For instance, in the representative RFM GR00T-N1.6, the action generation head consumes about 40% of overall inference time on a desktop GPU (NVIDIA L40) and up to 50% on an edge device for vehicles and robotics (NVIDIA Jetson Orin). To operate physical robots safely in real time, reducing the number of sampling steps to the absolute minimum is essential.

### The Promise of MeanFlow and Training Collapse in RFMs
In image generation, MeanFlow has recently emerged to enable one-step generation without distillation or complex regularizations. Instead of predicting the instantaneous velocity $\mathbf{v}_t$, it learns the "average velocity $\mathbf{u}_{t,r}$" between any two time steps. If this worked for robotics, an action could be produced from noise in a single forward pass. However, directly applying MeanFlow to RFMs causes training loss to spike wildly, leading to complete performance collapse.

### Two Distinctive Dynamics in the Velocity Field
When the authors compared the velocity fields of image generation (DiT on ImageNet) and robotics (SimVLA on LIBERO), crucial differences unique to robotics became apparent:
- **Surge in local acceleration**: In the late stage of denoising ($t < 0.3$), the rate of change of average velocity (local acceleration) surges sharply, reaching 76 times its initial value ($t=1$). Estimating the derivative term—which infers global trends from local observations—becomes exceptionally difficult.
- **Widening variance**: As denoising progresses, the spread (variance) of sample acceleration broadens. This becomes even more pronounced as task diversity increases.

Because MeanFlow relies on a "bootstrap" structure that uses its own predicted derivatives to create target signals, these two factors cause small initial estimation errors to amplify exponentially, collapsing training. To overcome this, the authors designed Kinematic MeanFlow (K-MF), which splits the time interval using a kinematic identity.

While image generation (blue) stays flat, robotics (red) surges 76-fold near the end with expanding variance. Right (b): The resulting loss landscapes; K-MF (right) completely smooths out the severe spikes observed in MeanFlow (center).

sections.heading: The Evolution of Fast Sampling and Robotics' Unexplored Challenge
sections.summary: Fast sampling for diffusion and flow models has been pursued via distillation, Consistency Models, and MeanFlow. However, prior efforts focused predominantly on image generation or single-task specialist robot policies. One-step methods tailored to the unique dynamics of generalist RFMs handling diverse tasks remained unexplored.
sections.details:
### Fast Sampling Techniques in Image Generation
Reducing inference steps in diffusion and flow models has been actively studied primarily in image generation. Prominent methods include score/flow distillation, which trains few-step student models to mimic multi-step outputs, and Consistency Models, which directly predict the same trajectory endpoint from different points along the path. Recently, MeanFlow has garnered attention as a breakthrough framework that enables one-step generation from scratch without post-hoc distillation by directly learning the average velocity between two points. While a few works explore interval splitting, their goals are improving training efficiency or curriculum learning for images, differing fundamentally from the challenges in robotic velocity fields.

### Evolution of Action Generation Policies in Robotics
In robotics, Diffusion Policy pioneered the adoption of diffusion models, followed by fast-sampling variants such as Consistency Policy and FlowPolicy in imitation and reinforcement learning. Attempts to adapt MeanFlow to action generation (e.g., MP1, MVP, MeanflowQL) have also emerged, but they were confined to "specialist policies" trained on specific single tasks. Under single tasks with low data variance, naive MeanFlow can manage to operate, but it fails completely on "generalist RFMs" trained on diverse datasets. This work is the first to uncover the extreme velocity field dynamics in RFMs and make one-step generation viable for generalist foundation models.

sections.heading: Kinematic MeanFlow: Decoupling Derivatives with a Kinematic Identity
sections.summary: Starting from the definition of average velocity and MeanFlow mathematics, we introduce a kinematic identity that divides the time interval into two sub-intervals at an intermediate point. This decouples the time derivative term into early and late segments, preventing error amplification at its source. A lightweight learnable generator dynamically sets the intermediate point, balancing efficiency and stability.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Preliminaries: Formulations of Flow Matching and MeanFlow
A standard RFM takes vision and language features along with current robot states to output future action sequences (action chunks $\mathbf{a}$). Flow Matching trains the network to predict the instantaneous velocity $\mathbf{v}_t = \bm{\epsilon} - \mathbf{a}$ along a straight trajectory $\mathbf{z}_t = (1-t)\mathbf{a} + t\bm{\epsilon}$ connecting noise $\bm{\epsilon}$ and action $\mathbf{a}$.

In contrast, MeanFlow considers the "average velocity $\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{z}_t, r, t)$" between any two time steps $r, t$ ($0 \le r \le t \le 1$). From fundamental kinematic relationships, average velocity can be expressed using instantaneous velocity and a time derivative term:
$$\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{z}_t, r, t) = \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{z}_t, t) + (t-r)\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{z}_t, r, t)$$
During training, the model $\pi_\theta$ is optimized against a regression target formed by applying the stop-gradient operator $\text{sg}(\cdot)$ to the right-hand side. At inference, simply setting $t=1, r=0$ yields actions via a single forward pass: $\hat{\mathbf{a}} = \mathbf{z}_1 - \pi_\theta(\mathbf{z}_1, 0, 1)$.

### 3.2 Core Idea of Kinematic MeanFlow (K-MF)
The breakdown of MeanFlow training stems from severe estimation errors in the time derivative term $\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}_{t,r}$ on the right-hand side, caused by late-stage acceleration surges and widening variance. To counter this, the authors utilize a "kinematic identity" stating that at any intermediate point $c \in (r, t)$, the average velocity can be strictly expressed as a convex combination of two sub-intervals:
$$\mathbf{u}_{t,r} = \frac{t-c}{t-r}\mathbf{u}_{t,c} + \frac{c-r}{t-r}\mathbf{u}_{c,r}$$
Defining the time ratio as $\lambda = (c-r)/(t-r)$, the overall time derivative term cleanly separates into two derivative terms for the first and second intervals:
$$\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}_{t,r} = (1-\lambda)^2\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}_{t,c} + \lambda^2\frac{d}{dc}\mathbf{u}_{c,r}$$
This works because the early derivative term $\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}_{t,c}$ captures the stable early stage, while the late derivative term $\frac{d}{dc}\mathbf{u}_{c,r}$ focuses exclusively on the late-stage variations. The intermediate point $c$ acts as an anchor that prevents errors from snowballing.

### How to Choose the Intermediate Point $c$?
Three strategies were explored for selecting the interval splitting ratio $\lambda$:
- **Random Sampling**: Sampled from a uniform distribution $\lambda \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)$, serving as a baseline to evaluate splitting diversity.
- **Fixed Midpoint**: Fixed at $\lambda = 0.5$ at all times, a straightforward design that eliminates extra variance.
- **Learnable Strategy (LS)**: Dynamically predicted using a lightweight 3-layer MLP $G_\phi(t, r)$. It is optimized via a loss function $\mathcal{L}_{\text{gen}}$ designed to keep decoupled estimates away from global estimates early in training to curb bootstrap error, while driving both toward alignment late in training to foster self-consistency.

### Fast Implementation Techniques
To compute time derivatives, Jacobian-Vector Products (JVPs) are evaluated using forward-mode automatic differentiation (dual numbers), executing in a single forward pass without constructing a backpropagation graph. Furthermore, because the two sub-intervals are mutually independent, they are batched together and computed in parallel, limiting the training time increase to within 33% relative to Flow Matching.

sections.heading: Surpassing Multi-Step with One Step: Rigorous Benchmark Evaluations
sections.summary: Using GR00T and SimVLA, we evaluated K-MF across LIBERO simulation, real-world datasets including Fractal and BridgeData V2, and navigation tasks. K-MF matched or exceeded multi-step Flow Matching in success rate with only one-step inference, while slashing action head latency by up to 74.4%.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Baselines
Evaluations used GR00T-N1.6 for pre-trained model fine-tuning and SimVLA-S for training from scratch. Four datasets differing in scale and morphology were tested: table-top simulation LIBERO (2,000 trajectories), real Google Robot data Fractal (87,000 trajectories), real WidowX data BridgeData V2 (53,000 trajectories), and quadruped Unitree G1 PointNav (658 trajectories). Baselines included multi-step Flow Matching (FM), standard MeanFlow, and existing variants $\alpha$-Flow and MVP.

### Preliminary Experiments: Limitations of Existing Methods
In preliminary tests on LIBERO-10, standard MeanFlow failed to match FM even with delicate tuning such as gradient clipping and progressive time-step sampling, achieving at best 2-step generation. Furthermore, $\alpha$-Flow experienced large performance drops at 1 step, and MVP failed to generate valid actions entirely. In contrast, only the proposed K-MF effortlessly reached success rates comparable to FM in a single step.

### Main Benchmark Results
- **LIBERO (Fine-tuning & Scratch)**: In GR00T fine-tuning, 1-step K-MF achieved 97.9% compared to FM's 95.9%. In SimVLA scratch training, K-MF reached 88.7% versus FM's 88.4%, demonstrating performance on par with or better than multi-step models.
- **Large-Scale Real-World Data (Fractal & BridgeData V2)**: In SimplerEnv-based real-to-sim transfer evaluations, K-MF achieved 68.0% on Fractal (GoogleX) versus FM's 61.5%, and 52.9% on BridgeData V2 (WidowX) versus FM's 50.5%, surpassing multi-step FM in both benchmarks using only 1-step generation.
- **Robot Navigation (PointNav)**: K-MF achieved 100% on in-distribution data and 76.5% on out-of-distribution unseen environments (hospital scenes) compared to FM's 70.5%, proving strong generalization capability.

### Inference Latency and Training Overhead
Inference benchmarking showed that action head latency dropped by 67.5%–74.4% on L40 GPUs and Jetson Orin edge devices. This led to a 30.3%–54.9% reduction in total end-to-end model latency, substantially increasing control frequency. Regarding training time, the overhead compared to FM was limited to 33% for GR00T and 27% for SimVLA, remaining well within practical limits.

captions.F5: In-depth velocity field dynamics of RFMs: (a) late-stage acceleration surges are consistent across different model architectures, (b) variance is wider in complex Fractal data than in simpler LIBERO data, and (c) local acceleration variance scales with the number of tasks following log and power laws.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: We uncovered the challenges of one-step action generation in RFMs through the lens of velocity field dynamics and solved them with K-MF by decoupling time derivatives kinematically. Despite minor training overhead and remaining extensions to whole-body control, this work marks a significant stride toward physical robot deployment.
sections.details:
### Conclusion
In this study, we introduced Kinematic MeanFlow (K-MF), a one-step action generation policy for generalist Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs). To eliminate the inference latency inherent in conventional Flow Matching, we identified the root causes—late-stage acceleration surges and widening variance—via detailed velocity field analysis. We resolved them through an elegant mathematical approach: decoupling derivative terms using a kinematic identity. Extensive experiments spanning multiple models, dataset scales, and robot embodiments demonstrated that K-MF surpasses multi-step models while running in a single step, yielding dramatic latency reductions.

### Limitations and Future Work
The paper highlights the following limitations:
- **Training Overhead**: While mitigated by computational graph optimizations, training time still increases by approximately 30% compared to Flow Matching.
- **Unexplored Control Domains**: Evaluations centered primarily on manipulation and wheeled navigation. Extending the approach to extremely high-degree-of-freedom tasks, such as whole-body coordination in humanoid robots or dexterous multi-fingered manipulation, remains an avenue for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix: Why Do Errors Amplify? Physical Velocity Field Mechanisms
sections.summary: The appendix presents simulation analyses on late-stage error amplification and breaks down rate-of-change differences in speed and angle between robotics and image models. It also highlights the importance of 'complete decoupling' by sampling intermediate states from ground-truth trajectories.
sections.details:
### Late-Stage Error Amplification Simulation
We measured the effect on the final time derivative term when injecting a tiny 1% perturbation into the latent variable $\mathbf{z}_t$ at each denoising step. Results revealed that minor noise injected early in denoising amplified by up to 120 times by the end of the process. Both theoretical and experimental analyses confirm that K-MF confines this multiplicative error accumulation into small additive errors by splitting the time interval and computing sub-intervals independently.

### Why Is One-Step Generation Harder in Robotics than in Images?
In standard Flow Matching, robotics is known to require fewer sampling steps than image generation. Why, then, is one-step generation so much harder in robotics?

By decomposing the velocity vector's rate of change into "magnitude (speed) change" and "angle (direction) change," the authors observed that early in denoising, robotic velocity fields show almost no change in either direction or magnitude, following nearly straight trajectories. This explains why coarse multi-step sampling worked easily. However, immediately before reaching target actions near the end of denoising, both speed and angle undergo extreme, sudden shifts. This steep non-linearity causes fatal errors when MeanFlow attempts to infer global integrals from local derivative observations.

### Complete Decoupling via Ground-Truth Trajectory Sampling
When obtaining intermediate states $\mathbf{z}_c$, the method samples directly from the conditional flow trajectory $\mathbf{z}_c = (1-c)\mathbf{a} + c\bm{\epsilon}$ based on ground truth, rather than using the model's own predicted trajectory. Using predicted trajectories would allow early prediction errors to corrupt intermediate states, directly undermining subsequent derivative calculations. Anchoring to ground-truth data completely decouples the two sub-intervals, severing error propagation while enabling parallel computation for faster training.

captions.F8: Relative error amplification ratio across denoising steps. A mere 1% noise injected in early steps (around $t=1.0$) amplifies sharply by approximately 120 times toward the end of denoising ($r \to 0$).
captions.F9: Comparison of local acceleration, speed change rate, and angular change rate between a robotics model (top: SimVLA-S) and an image generation model (bottom: DiT-B). Robotics models exhibit an explosive surge in both speed and angle near the end, whereas image models remain gentle throughout.

takeaways: When porting popular computer vision methods (such as MeanFlow) to robotics, one must account for robotics-specific velocity field dynamics: sharp, late-stage shifts in speed and angle.
Error amplification in bootstrap-style learning can be prevented effectively by splitting intervals via kinematic identities and anchoring intermediate states to ground-truth trajectories.
Adopting a one-step generation policy reduces end-to-end inference latency by 30%–50% without sacrificing performance, making high-frequency real-time control on edge devices practical.
limitations: Evaluating multiple Jacobian-Vector Products (JVPs) increases training duration by approximately 30% compared to Flow Matching.
Validation is limited to table-top manipulation and mobile robot navigation; efficacy in humanoid whole-body control or complex multi-fingered dexterous manipulation remains unverified.
